Md Hefzul Bari Advocate with Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury, Advocate with Imranul Kabir, Advocate and Reja-e-Rabbi, Advocate—For the Opposite Party No.2.

Md Fazlur Rahman Khan, DAG with Md Shafiqul Islam Siddique DAG with Md Jahir Ahmed, AAG and Md Ruhul Amin, AAG—For the State-Opposite Party.

full_judgment:
AKM Abdul Hakim, J: On an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure filed by the accused-petitioner, Md Shahabuddin Alam, a Rule was issued on 17-4-2019 calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the proceeding of CR Case No. 2607 of 2018 (Kotwali) under section 406/420/ 422/109/120B/34 of the Penal Code, 1860, now pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chattogram, should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Facts of the case, relevant for disposal of the Rule, may be briefly stated as follows: 

 One Syed Md Tanjim Hossain, Senior Vice-President and Assistant Manager, Dhaka Bank Ltd. Khatungonj Branch filed a petition of complainant being CR Case No. 2607 of 2018 (Kotwali) before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court, Chattagram against the accused-petitioner and Mrs Yasmin Alam under sections 406/420/422/109/120B/34 of the Penal Code on 27-12-2018 alleging, inter-alia , that the accused-petitioner is the Managing Director of SA Oil Refinery Ltd and Samannaz Super Oil Ltd and it used to import Crude Oil from abroad under L/C facilities through the complainant Bank and after refined sell the Palm Oil in the Local Market; that it further alleged that on 7-9-2000 out of the two companies of the accused, SA Oil Refinery Ltd. submitted an application to the complainant-bank to open L/C for importing Crude Oil and other goods; that in support of its loan application, to create bank's trust and confidence in respect of their company's business stability, they have created necessary documents; that thereafter, bank on good faith sanctioned loan on 5-9-2001 in favour of the accused-petitioner's company for an amount of Taka 40 crore on L/C Account, 10 crore on LTR Account and Taka 1 crore on Bank Guarantee Account; that against the said loan the company executed necessary charge documents in favour of the bank; that specially bank disbursed the loan amount on the basis of Trust Receipts and Personal Guarantee executed by the company and the accuseds; that since the accuseds did not pay the loan amount within the specified period fixed in the sanction letter, but the accused just for embezzling loan money by false temptation and with ill intention made part payment; that on the prayer of the accuseds, bank renewed its earlier loan and further granted new facilities; that ultimately when the company of the accuseds became defaulter, on its prayer dated 30-4-2015, bank on the basis of the Letter dated 14-10-2015, all the loan liabilities including interest amount was re-scheduled and accuseds were given opportunity to pay off its loan; that on 18-1-2016 an Agreement was executed between the bank and the accuseds but they failed to pay the loan amount of the bank as per agreement, that lastly when the accuseds refused to pay the bank dues, the bank through its Advocate sent Legal Notice to them on 5-4-2018. In this way the accuseds has committed breach of trust by misappropriating bank's outstanding loan money to the extent of Taka 247,24,84,766.49 only upto 24-4-2018 and cheated the Bank. Thus the accused has committed offence under section 406/420/422/109/120B/34 of the Penal Code. 

 3. That after examining the opposite party No. 2 under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Chattagram by his order dated 27-12-2018 took cognizance of offence against the accused-petitioner and Mrs. Yasmin Alam under section 406/420/422/109/1208/34 of the Penal Code and issued Warrant of Arrest (W/A) against them and registered as CR Case No. 2607 of 2018 (Kotwali). 

 4. That it is stated that the accused-petitioner was arrested in connection with another case and then he was shown arrested in the instant case on 7-1-2019. That thereafter on 8-1-2019, the accused-petitioner prayed for bail before the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Cognizance Court, Kotwali, Chattogram. Prayer of his bail was refused on the same day. Then the accused petitioner filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 332 of 2019 before the learned Metropolitan Session Judge, Chattogram praying for bail but the same was rejected on 28-1-2019. Subsequently, the accused petitioner was granted bail by the Hon'ble High Court Division in Miscellaneous Case No. 8288 of 2019 on February 3, 2019. That thereafter on 25-3-2019, the accused petitioner appeared before the Metropolitan Magistrate Cognizance Court 2, Chattogram and filed hazira. Then next date of the case was fixed on 22-5-2019 for further hajira and for carrying out of warrant of arrest against another accused of the instant case. 

 5. That later on the petitioner filed an Supplementary Affidavit dated 21-1-2021 annexing some documents reiterating the statements made in the main application. It is stated that opposite party No. 2 earlier filed Artha Rin Suit No. 105 of 2018 against the petitioner and his company for realisation of loan amount of Taka 2,47,24,84,766.49 on 26-4-2018. The next date of the suit is fixed on 4-2-2021 for peremptory hearing. It is further stated that the opposite party No. 2-bank took 16 years to make up its mind and with ill motive and intention just to harass filed the instant CR Case against the accused-petitioner on 27-12-2018 alleging he has misappropriated the verbatimly same amount. Hence the initiation and continuation of the case is sheer abuse of the process of the court and same is liable to be quashed to secure the ends of justice. 

 7. In this case learned Advocate Mr Md Hefzul Bari filed a Vokalatnama on behalf of the complainant-Dhaka-Bank-opposite-party No. 2. Thereafter, when the matter was heard-in-part on 18-8-2021, learned Advocate Mr Imranul Kabir filed another Vokalatnama on behalf of the Bank-opposite-party No. 2. At the time of hearing learned Advocate Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury appeared and made extensive submissions for the bank-opposite party No. 2. 

 9. In the Counter-Affidavit dated 26-1-2021, the opposite-party No. 2 denying the material allegations made in the application and asserted that the accused-petitioner filed this application with an ulterior motive to delay the process of recovery of outstanding legal dues of a scheduled Bank. It is further stated that the petitioner has willfully mislead this court by making false and incorrect statements and by concealing and suppressing material facts with ill motive for lingering Bank's liabilities. That it is to be mentioned that so many suits/cases has been pending before various courts against the petitioner filed by the bank. 

 10. In the Supplementary Counter-Affidavit dated 24-6-2021 it was further asserted that the accused-petitioner obtained credit facilities from the bank. In pursuance of the terms of the said sanction letters the accused-petitioner in order to avail himself of the said credit facilities and security for securing the repayment of the said credit facilities, executed the charge/security documents as per sanction letters and the accused-petitioner had fully availed the credit facilities from the bank and he is under legal obligation to liquidate his outstanding dues but he did not liquidate his outstanding dues, inspite of bank's repeated requests, reminders and demands. The accused-petitioner had failed, neglected and defaulted intentionally to pay and adjust the said outstanding dues as such bank filed Artha Rin Suit, which is pending before the Artha Rin Adalat, Chattogram and several criminal cases also filed against accused-petitioner. 

 11. In filing Second Supplementary Counter-Affidavit dated 27-6-2021 the opposite-party No. 2 after denying the statements made in Paragraph No. 10 of the Criminal Miscellaneous petition further asserted that there is no legal bar in continuation of the Artha Rin Suit, CR Cases against dishonor of cheque and CR case out of criminal breach of trust arising out of LTR (Letter of Trust Receipt) and cheating arising out of the same transaction, same contract, if there are distinct cause of action(s) under the relevant particular law. When there is a default situation of LTR (Letter of Trust Receipt) and a borrower/ defaulter provides cheques for installments or down payments or any other valid purpose and if the said cheques are dishonoured and if the defaulter or borrower does not pay the installment amount/cheque amount upon receiving notice from the lender Bank, in such a situation, a lender Bank's Artha Rin Suit of the loan amount, CR cases for cheque dishonour and CR case for criminal breach of trust and cheating out of the LTR and other loans contract breaches are all maintainable. As such the instant Case is liable to be discharged. It was further stated that the petitioner's SA Oil Group was sanctioned LTR in the year 2001 which was breached by the petitioner. However, in order to recover public money, the opposite party No. 2-Bank converted LTR facility into a term loan upon petitioner's request. The petitioner did not intentionally repay any installment of the term loan. However, in order to recover public money, the opposite party No. 2 Bank, upon request of the petitioner on several occasions, rescheduled the petitioner's outstanding liability with the opposite party No. 2 Bank. However, the petitioner did not act upon conditions of the rescheduling sanction letters of the bank. Petitioner did not pay any installment amount as per revised repayment schedule. Each installment was Taka 2 crore and above. In the Rescheduling Sanction No. DBL/KTG/CR/2015/ 1562 dated October 14, 2015 it is stated that `Failure of pay two consecutive installments shall be considered as default and the restructured facilities will stand cancelled'. Since the petitioner did not pay even one installment, therefore the reschedule restructured facilities are to be cancelled against the petitioner. Hence, all the parties went back to the original positions. It means criminal breach of trust and cheating on part of the petitioner are subsisting. Therefore, CR Case out of criminal breach of trust and cheating under sections 406 and 420 of the Penal Code is maintainable. 

 14. The opposite-party No. 2 again filed Fourth Supplementary Counter-Affidavit on 17-8-2021 asserting that in the process of abuse of process of law, the accused-petitioner along with their two Companies, namely, SA Refinery Limited and Samannaz Super Oil Limited initiated two company cases, being; Company Matter No. 181 of 2018 and 182 of 2018 seeking winding up of those two companies. The accused-petitioner obtained Rule and Order of Stay on 16-5-2018 against hundreds of Statutory Tribunal Cases and Complaint Register cases, all filed by various banks to whom the accused-petitioner owes huge amount of loans. The accused-petitioner obtained orders restraining all further proceedings of any suits or proceedings including all criminal proceedings against the company in the said Company Matters. 

 16. Mr Subrata Kumar Kundu, learned Advocate appearing for the accused-petitioner after placing the complaint petition submits that the allegations contained in the complaint, are civil in nature, even if, are taken as true do not constitute an offence punishable under section 406/420 of the Penal Code and, as such, the impugned proceeding is liable to be quashed to secure the ends of justice. In this connection learned Advocate referred the decisions reported in 50 DLR (AD) 163, 4 BLT (AD) 231, 23 BLT (AD) 76. He further submits that admittedly the accused-petitioner's company took loan from the bank and they made part payment to the bank against the loan amount and interest and there is no initial intention of deception on the part of the petitioner in committing offence under section 406/420 of the Penal Code. In this respect he relied on the decisions reported in 19 BLD (AD) 128 = 4 BLC (AD) 167, 45 DLR (AD) 26 and 53 DLR 283. He candidly submits that admittedly, the petitioner's company after taking loan made part payment of loan together with interest to the bank and, as such, it cannot be said the accused-petitioner had mens rea to deceive the bank in not making payment of the rest loan amount and interest. In the absence of mens rea and inability to fulfill a promise or breach of contract does not constitute an offence of cheating. In this regard, he cited a decision of 5 BLC 380. Learned Advocate finally submits that the complainant opposite party No. 2 filed the present complaint long after 14 years from the first date of occurrence (4-3-2002). Moreover before filing the complaint, the opposite party No. 2 also filed Artha Rin Suit No 105 of 2018 on 26-4-2018 against the accused-petitioner and his company and others in the Artha Rin Adalat for recovery of self same amount Taka 247,24,84,766.49, same is now pending for peremptory hearing, filing of cases on the same matter is tantamount to double jeopardy. Hence the proceeding is liable to be quashed and the Rule is liable to be made absolute. 

 17. On the contrary, the learned Advocate Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury for the opposite party No. 2-Dhaka Bank opposed the Rule. He emphatically argued that the accused-petitioner having induced the bank for getting the loan amount of Taka 247,24,84,766.49 and never had the intention to repay the loan and interest even though several requests were made to them. The learned Advocate further pressed that whether the intention was to cheat from the inception or not is a question of fact and same can only be decided at the time of trial after appreciating the evidence. The learned counsel submits that there being allegations of cheating and forgery and also allegation of using forged document for the purpose of securing loan and as the allegations made against the accused-petitioner in the complaint constitutes offence under the Penal Code on the face of it, unless the complainant is allowed to adduce evidence in the trial it can not be said that the petitioner has committed no offence and, therefore, to quash the proceeding at this stage will amount to stifling the complainant. He next submits that the pendency of civil suit can not bar the proceedings of criminal case for criminal offence. There is no legal impediments to file criminal case even a civil suit is pending on the self same allegations. He also submits that the accused-petitioner invoke extra-ordinary jurisdiction under section 561A is not maintainable as it filed very initial stage just after taking cognizance by the Metropolitan Magistrate without availing the available remedies which is appears to be a prematured one. He next submits that quashment of proceedings at the stage before framing charge is not permissible and, as such, the instant application filed under section 561A should be rejected. He lastly submits that the facts of the present case is not preposterous, groundless. There is no abuse of process of any court and ends of justice requires that the accused be tried and punished for embezzling public funds and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. In support of his submissions learned Advocate cited following decisions namely: 13 MLR 2008 (AD) 184, 54 DLR 114, 62 DLR (AD) 233, 64 DLR 393. 

 20. The moot question before us is whether the petition of complaint contain the allegations and statements which, on the face of it, constitute a criminal offence under the Penal Code against the petitioner and if the answer is in the negative, then whether the exercise of the powers of this court under its extra-ordinary jurisdiction as provided under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure will be called for to quash the proceeding before allowing the complainant to lead evidence to prove its case. Along with the above point another question arises for our consideration is whether institution and pendency of the civil suit claiming the dues on account of loan taken by the company will itself be a bar for the criminal proceeding. 

 22. The consensus of judicial opinion is that it is not possible, desirable or expedient to lay down any inflexible Rule which should govern the exercise of this inherent jurisdiction. The exercise of this jurisdiction will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. 

 24. The pertinent question having arisen and posed as to when and under what circumstances the inherent jurisdiction can and should be exercised by the High Court Division, Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J. speaking for the court in the case of Abdul Quader Choudhury and others vs The State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 the apex court considered the question as to when and under what circumstances the inherent jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can and should be exercised to quash the proceeding. It was observed: "Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the court" 

 "Cases may also arise where the allegations in the first information report or the complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not constitute the offence alleged, in such cases no question of appreciating evidence arises, it is a matter merely of looking at the complaint or the First Information Report to decide whether the offence alleged is disclosed or not. In such cases it would be legitimate for the High Court to hold that it would be manifestly unjust to allow process of the criminal court to be issued against the accused person." (emphasis supplied) 

 26. Relying on the above noted passages of the case reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38, it transpires that the instant case falls within the category of cases where interference of this Court by exercising its inherent power has become not only necessary but also imperative to prevent the abuse of the process of the court. 

 27. Similar view on the principles of quashing the proceedings was, subsequently, followed in the decision in the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, 1997 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16. 

 28. In the case of Bangladesh vs Tan Kheng Hock, 31 DLR (AD) 69 charge-sheet was submitted under sections 156(8) and 156(89) of the Customs Act read with section 25B of the Special Powers Act, 1974. The High Court Division interfered at the stage when only charge-sheet was submitted but before taking cognizance of the offence by the court competent to try the case. The Appellate Division considered facts of the case and a good number of decisions including Emperor vs Khawaja Nazir Ahmed AIR 1945 Privy Council 19, Raja Hog Newaz vs Mohd. Afzal, 19 DLR (SC) 369, Abdul Quader Chowdhury and others vs The State, 28 DLR (AD) 38. While allowing the appeals, it was held- 

 "The case is yet to be sent to the appropriate Court for trial after taking cognizance. It is an established principle that ordinarily proceedings instituted alleging criminal offence must be tired in accordance with law and the same should not be  interfered with at an interlocutory stage or even at the early stage in exercise of the  inherent jurisdiction of the High Court under section 56IA of the Code, of course, facts of a particular case may call for interference  under section 561A of the Code where even  on the admitted facts no criminal case stands  against the accused, and further prolongation  of the prosecution would amount to  harassment to an innocent person that is  abuse of the process of the Court." 

 "In the instant case the question so far is one of investigation, because, no prosecution has yet been commenced, and we have not the slightest hesitation to hold that the High Court Division quashed the proceedings in erroneous exercise of its inherent power under section 561A of the Code." 

 31. In the case of Sher Ali (Md) and others vs State, 46 DLR (AD) 67 it has been decided: 

 32. In order to dispose of this Rule, let us now examine whether the facts of the present case attracts any of the ingredients of sections 405 and 415 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 34. Keeping in view the relevant provisions of law, we want to discuss whether the petition of complaint discloses a prima facie offence of cheating against the accused-petitioner in the instant case or not. 

 36. By referring the undisputed fact of part payment learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to a decision in the case of Abdul Rauf vs State, 53 DLR (2001) 283, wherein it has been spelt out: 

 37. In the decision in the case of Dewan Obaidur Rahman vs State, 1999 BLD (AD) 128 = 4 BLC (AD) 167 relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, it has been laid down: 

 38. Apart from the aforesaid facts and legal aspects of the case, it is not alleged in the complaint petition that the accused-petitioner and others refused to pay off the loan amount and interest to the bank. Thus it is evidently clear from the complaint petition that accused-petitioner never refused to pay up the remaining loan amount along with interest to the bank. Furthermore, the complainant-Bank already filed Artha Rin Case No. 105 of 2018 before the Artha Rin Adalat, Chattogram on 26-4-2018 before filing of the petition of complaint on 27-12-2018 for realization of selfsame amount. Thus it reveals that there is no offence of cheating under section 420 of the penal Code against the accused-petitioner. In the case of Rafique (Md) vs Syed Morshed Hossain and another reported in 50 DLR (AD) 163, it has been decided: 

 39. Moreover, our Apex Court in a number of cases has usually cautioned against criminalizing civil disputes, such as breach of contractual obligations. The legislature intended to criminalize only those breaches which are accompanied by fraudulent, dishonest or deceptive inducements, which resulted involuntary and inefficient transfers, under section 415 of Penal Code. 

 40. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case and the propositions of law cited above and from a clear reading of petition of quashment, Counter-Affidavits and Supplementary Counter-Affidavit with annexures, we do not find any element of initial intention of deception, which constitutes an offence of cheating against the accused-petitioner. 

 43. On the face of the allegations in the Petition of Complaint, we notice that the accused-petitioner's company took loan from the bank. It is a settled principle of law that the transaction of loan money under a loan agreement do not operate as an entrustment under section 405 of the Penal Code. Accordingly, when there is no entrustment, there cannot be any trust. If there is no trust, there cannot be a question of criminal breach of trust. In the transaction of loan, the loan giver does not hold any control of the loan amount and, as such, it constitutes no breach of trust. If there is any breach of contract, the remedy lies in the civil suit and that no criminal case would lie against the accused-petitioner for violation of terms and conditions of loan agreement mere breach of promise, agreement or contract does not, ipso facto, constitute the offence of the criminal breach of trust under section 405 of the Penal Code without there being a clear case of entrustment. It will be seen that the impugned proceedings in the facts and circumstances of the case is entirely misconceived because the allegations that the loan dues were allowed to accrue dishonestly does neither attract an offence under section 420 nor section 406 of the Penal Code or under any other section. 

 44. In Shamsul Alam and others vs AFA Hassan and others, 40 DLR 46, which was a case under sections 406 and 420 of the Penal, a question arose whether 'loan money' constituted `entrustment' within the meaning of section 405. The proceeding was quashed. It was held, 

 45. The same principle was applied in Reazuddin Ahmed (Md) vs State and another 49 DLR (AD) 64. In this case the trial was held in absentia and the appellant was convicted under section 406 of the Penal Code. It was held, 

 47. In the case of MA Sukkur vs Md Zahirul Haque and another reported in 2015 (23) BLT (AD) 76. In this case, the appellant took loan from Bangladesh Shilpa Bank (BSB) and he defaulted in making payment of loan money. Charge was framed under section 420 of the Penal Code. It has been held— 

 "It appears that dispute, if any, between the parties is of civil nature and complainant-Bank already instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1992 for realization of outstanding loan dues from the appellant. There is not gainsaying the fact that the dispute arose out of money given to the appellant and, as such  it appears that criminal proceeding against the appellant is an abuse of the process of court-The normal financial transaction between the debtor and creditor does not come within the scope of the offence". 

 48. Be that as it may, the proposition of law is well settled that civil claim and civil dispute to be settled and sorted out in civil court, it can not be brought in criminal court as a contrivance to put pressure upon a party. This is the rarest of the rare cases, "out of a thousand" where even at the initial stage we can interfere in exercise of the inherent jurisdiction provided section 561A of the Code to secure ends of justice and to abuse of the process of the court. 

 50. The learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2 by referring the decisions of our Apex Court in the case of Abdul Huque reported in 60 DLR (AD) 1 and Engineer Mosharrqf Hossen, 21 BLC (AD) 211 tried to submits that before taking cognizance of a case by the competent Court or Tribunal a proceedings cannot be said to be pending and accordingly, a proceedings cannot be quashed unless cognizance is taken in respect thereof and has been taken and process issued. In the cited cases the accused petitioner seeking quashment of the proceedings under section 409/420/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In both the cases, the petitioners seeking quashing of the proceeding were preferred before taking cognizance of the offence by the Senior Metro-politan Special Judge, who had the exclusive jurisdiction to take cognizance. That the law declared in the above cited cases, which are Anti-Corruption cases, should be confined to the facts and circumstances of those cases. In the present case cognizance has been taken and process issued thereupon by the learned Magistrate. It is relevant to mention that both in 21 BLC (AD) and 60 DLR (AD) case, the apex court refrained from dwelling upon the issue as to whether the FIR story disclosed any offence. 

 51. In the case of Syed Mohammad Hashem alias Hashim vs State reported in 48 DLR (AD) 87 the Appellate Division held— 

 52. In the case of Nasiruddin Mahmud and others vs Momtazuddin Ahmed and another reported in 36 DLR (AD) 14 = 1984 BLD (AD) 97 the Appellate Division observed in paragraph No. 29— 

 "Proceeding before a court starts when the Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on police report or on complaint. Before such cognizance, there is no proceedings that may be quashed under section 561 A of the CrPC". Accordingly, before taking of cognizance of a case by the complainant court or tribunal a proceeding cannot be said to be pending and accordingly, a proceeding cannot be quashed unless cognizance in respect thereof has been taken and process issued. 

 53. In the present case, learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Chattogram took cognizance of the offence against the accused-petitioner and another under section 406/420/422/109/120B/34 of the Penal Code on 27-12-2018, issued W/A against them and same was pending before the Magistrate Court. 

 54. Learned Advocate for the opposite party Mr Imranul Kabir by referring a unreported judgment dated 1-12-2020 of the Appellate Division in the case of Mohammad Amir Ali Mostafa vs Shah Md Nurul Alam and others candidly submits that without availing the other remedy accused is not allowed to move under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 55. In the cited case the complaint appellant filed CR Case No. 1966 of 2005 against the accused-respondents under section 420/467/468/ 471 of the Penal Code before the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, who after examining the petitioner under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by order dated 9-11-2005 gave a direction for holding judicial inquiry. Then on 28-2-2006 learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka after taking deposition of five witnesses including the petitioners submitted a report to the effect that offence under section 467/471 of the Penal Code has been proved against the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as they created forged deed and the respondent nos. 3 and 4 as they are witnesses to the said deed. Then on 7-3-2008, the learned Magistrate on the basis of the said report took cognizance of the case under section 467/471 of the Penal Code and issued summons against the respondent Nos. 1-4. But the respondents without appearing before the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka filed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 1966 of 2005 before the High Court Division whereupon Rule was issued on 13-6-2006 and the Rule was made absolute on 27-3-2018 and proceedings was quashed. Against the judgment of the High Court Division complainant filed the instant appeal before the Appellate Division. Their Lordships allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment order of the High Court dated 27-3-2008 by taking into consideration to another decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Habibur Rahman Mollah (Ex-Member of Parliament Dhaka-4) vs State and another reported in 62 DLR (AD) 233. 

 56. In the case of Habibur Rahman Mollah reported in 62 DLR (AD) 233 their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that Durnity Daman Commission lodged FIR on 3-10-2007 against the petitioner for commission of offences punishable under section 26(1) and 27(1) of Durnity Daman Commission Ain, 2004 read with rule 15 Gha(5) of the Emergency Powers Rules, 2007. Thereafter he moved High Court Division when good number of witness have been examined and cross-examined, prosecution case is almost over as such High Court Division find any urged to invoke inherent jurisdiction to quash the proceeding and discharged the Rule. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division dismissed the appeal by observing that the learned Judges of the High Court Division in the process are perfectly justified refusing to exercise therein inherent power in the facts circumstances of the case. 

 57. Mr Imranul Kabir further argues that in XVI ADC 326, the Apex Court refused to quash the proceedings on the ground that cognizance of the offence was not taken yet. Thus argument is misconceived one. In the said case their lordships considered the allegations made in the FIR and found that the FIR disclosed prima facie offence under section 420/466/467/468/47 of the Penal Code and same is pending for holding investigations. The fact that cognizance of the offence was not taken yet was not the ground for refusal to quash the proceeding. 

 58. It appears that the facts and circumstances and points of law in the aforesaid cited case including the case of Habibur Rahman Mollah vs The State has no nexus in the facts and circumstances of the case in hand. In the cited cages prima facie offence has been disclosed but in the present case no offence has been disclosed from the facts stated in the complaint. 

 59. Learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2-Bank emphatically submits that there is not legal bar to file criminal case even a civil suit is pending on the self-same allegations. In support of his submissions he relied on the decisions of 63 DLR (AD) 79 and 13 BLC (AD). 65. We are totally at per with the settled principle of law as laid down by our Apex Court. But as we have already observed that in the instant case the allegations as stated in the complaint does not disclosed the ingredients of offence punishable under section 406/420 of the Penal Code are present. As such the principles enunciated in those decisions in no way help the informant-opposite-party No. 2. 

 60. In the present case the petitioner invoked jurisdiction for quashment of the proceedings when learned Magistrate took cognizance against the accused-petitioner for commission of offence punishable under sections 406/420/422/109/ 120B/34 of the Penal Code and issued process by order dated 27-12-2018 where the allegations in the complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged. Thus it cannot said that filing of the present case under section 561A of the Code is a prematured one. 

 61. As regards other decisions cited by the learned Advocate of the opposite-party No. 2 reported in 13 MLR (AD) 184, 13 MLR (HCD) 261, 54 DLR 114 and 64 DLR 393. We have carefully examined the decisions and found that the principles enunciated in those decisions in no way help the informant-opposite party No. 2 in the facts and circumstances of the present case and do not apply to the case under adjudication. 

 63. For the foregoing reasons, we hold that further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to unnecessary harassment to the accused-petitioner, that is, abuse of the process of the court. For securing ends of justice the present proceedings against the accused-petitioner is liable to be quashed. Accordingly, the criminal proceeding being CR Case No. 2607 of 2018 (Kotwali) under section 406/420/422/109/120B/ 34 of the Penal Code, 1860, now pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chattogram in so far it relates to the accused-petitioner, is hereby quashed.
